title: Father Zosima
hookLine: Dostoevsky's holy elder teaches that each of us is responsible for all

cards: A young army officer comes home in a rage the night before a duel. His orderly, a servant named Afanasy, does something small that annoys him, and the officer hits him in the face, hard, twice.

Afanasy just stands there and takes it. In the morning the officer wakes early and steps to the window. The sun is coming up over the garden, the birds are singing, and something cuts into him like a knife.

He remembers Afanasy standing there, arms at his sides, not even daring to lift a hand. This story is told inside a novel by the Russian writer Dostoevsky, by an old monk looking back on his own youth.

teach.b: Father Zosima is a character in The Brothers Karamazov, an elder in a Russian monastery, sought out by townspeople for counsel. He isn't a historical saint; he's Dostoevsky's picture of one.
At the heart of his teaching is a thought he first heard from his older brother, Markel, who was dying young.
Markel tells their mother that each of us is guilty before everyone, for everyone and everything, and that he is the most guilty of all. The grown-ups think it's the illness talking.
Years later, at that window, the young officer finally understands. He runs to Afanasy, bows to the ground, and asks his forgiveness.

teach.h: A BOW, AND A PISTOL THROWN AWAY.
teach.b: Then he goes to the duel, lets his opponent fire first, throws his own pistol away, and asks forgiveness of him too. His fellow officers are scandalized. He leaves the army, and in time becomes a monk.
As an old man, Zosima teaches it plainly, paraphrased: each of us is responsible for all, for everyone and everything. He doesn't mean that each person caused every wrong.

He means no one can say a suffering is none of their business. Every word, look and act goes out into the world and touches others. So for Zosima, the way out of blame and despair is to take on a share of the weight.

Paul wrote something close, in the King James Bible: "Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ." Zosima goes one step further: not only helping carry the burden, but treating it as partly your own.

how: Some readers, Orthodox and others, turn to Zosima's teachings in The Brothers Karamazov as a picture of the Russian elder tradition, sometimes alongside Paul's call to bear one another's burdens.

games.q: you're the young officer. last night you struck your servant. this morning, at the window, you're ashamed. the duel is in an hour. what do you do?
o: go to the duel and put it out of your mind.
run to your servant and bow down to ask his forgiveness.
pay him extra and say nothing.
games.why: he bowed to the ground before Afanasy and asked forgiveness, then at the duel threw his pistol away.

practice: Bring to mind a problem that belongs to everyone and so to no one: the shared kitchen, a neighbor nobody checks on, a family tension. Notice the voice that says, not my job, then quietly claim one piece of it, small enough to hold.
If you pray, offer it to God; if you don't, simply accept your share.

wordCard.voice: Father Zosima. The holy elder in Dostoevsky's novel, who learned from his dying brother that each of us is responsible for all.

orig.note: Greek: carry, bear — Paul's word in Galatians 6:2, bear ye one another's burdens.
